## RESEARCH PREVIEW: PIKA ENACT

## Creating Scenes that Respond to You

November 19, 2026. By the Pika Labs team

At Pika, we believe the next generation of AI creation should go beyond the prompt box, and more closely resemble how we already make films. Pika Enact is an exciting step in that direction.

Pika Enact is designed to mimic the experience of directing on set. It’s an experimental live-streaming environment built on Pika H3 Flex that generates video and sound in sub-second chunks, carrying scene context forward while incorporating new direction into the ongoing generation.

This allows the creator to interact with “actors,” manually re-stage a scene, and manipulate the camera—all in real time.

[insert launch video here]

## The technology enables three new modes of interaction:

• Live Staging . Place and reposition actors or objects within a running video with your mouse. The scene continues while you move them.

• Live Actor Direction: Speak directly to actors on set, and they’ll respond conversationally. Give them notes about dialogue, emotion, or movement, and they’ll enact them. Call “Action” to turn the rehearsal into a fresh, continuous take, and the actors will remember everything you’ve discussed.

• Live Camera Control . Direct camera movement with your mouse around a live, playing scene.

Below, we walk through each one: the data they learn from, their technical architecture, and some demo videos.

## Live Staging

Scene design and actor blocking are mainstays of a live directing experience. But AI video creation makes that process inexact and time-consuming. With Live Staging, rather than waiting for a generation to load in order to see the outcome of your direction, you get instantaneous feedback; you can manually shape the scene as it plays.

The live staging within Pika Enact lets the creator drag an object or actor into place with their mouse, which creates several key benefits:

• Precise placement: Where a prompt can only suggest “a bit to the left,” a cursor drags subjects to the exact intended spot.

• Consistency with environment: The model generates whatever you move—a person or a chair—together with the rest of the scene. As you drag, the subject responds naturally to the movement, while its pose, lighting, and shadows adapt to its surroundings. The result has no cut-out edges, no hole where it stood, and no compositing pass to clean up afterwards.

• Real-time responsiveness : The video keeps playing while you drag, and on a single server the model generates it 1.8× faster than it plays. Additionally, the subject actively reacts to being moved, shifting weight and adjusting posture mid-air before settling naturally where you let go.

To keep up with the cursor movement, we distill the model to a few steps and stream the mouse input and decoding in small pieces. In our low-latency setting, the picture responds in under 0.4 seconds on H100 , decoding included.

## The Data Engine

Training interactive video dragging requires strictly consistent before-and-after video pairs synchronized with frame-level cursor trajectories, which real-world footage cannot provide.

We built a physics-driven synthetic data engine to solve this. Starting from an untouched video, we animate a 3D stand-in along a drag path to simulate natural weight and momentum. Our video models then render photorealistic target clips while automatically logging mouse positions and button states.

This produces scalable, zero-labeling training pairs where only the dragged subject changes, covering lifting, multi-step carries, and inserting new subjects from photos into live scenes. The dataset drives our entire pipeline, from full-clip training and real-time distillation to evaluation.

For data access or more detail on how the data was made, contact our team at enterprise@pika.art .

## Technical Architecture

To make Pika H3 Flex draggable in real time, it has to learn two things: follow a cursor, and generate a stream instead of a clip.

Dragging trajectory: following your cursor. To follow a drag, the model has to know three things at every moment: what your mouse is doing, where it is, and what the scene would look like if you left it alone. Each comes in as its own signal. The mouse is sampled 24 times per second, and its button state and motion guide how the grabbed person or object moves at that exact moment. The cursor's position is marked on a heatmap over the frame, so the model knows precisely which spot you grabbed. The untouched video is fed in frame by frame alongside, so everything you don't touch stays as it was. All three enter H3 Flex through small new modules that start from zero, so the model learns to follow your hand while keeping H3 Flex's look.

From a clip to a stream. A model that generates the whole clip at once can't react to you: you would have to finish the drag before it starts, then wait seconds for the result. And when you're holding someone with your mouse, even a 0.7 s delay already feels sluggish. So we cut the video into short chunks and let each chunk look only at the past; the shorter the chunk, the sooner the picture can answer (0.7 s in the main model, 0.17 s in our low-latency model). This is how a language model writes one token at a time, and it brings the same tool: a key-value cache. Each new chunk reads the prompt and source video, the first chunk of the session, and the four most recent chunks from the cache; older chunks drop out. Positions are re-based every chunk so they never grow, which lets a session run indefinitely at constant cost. We first train this causal model on real history (teacher forcing).

But streaming alone isn’t enough. Each chunk still takes around twenty steps, and once the model reads its own output instead of real footage, small errors pile up from chunk to chunk.
